scenes.text:
They're saying in the square that the knocking has stopped. The first third night in three hundred years that nobody had to count.

Do you still have the journal? Turn to the lambing entry. "He is nine, grey-eyed, quick with his right hand and quicker to laugh."

Everybody is going to remember the thing you fought down there. Somebody ought to remember that one as well. I'll do it, if you like. I'm good with the ones nobody else sits up for.

Mind the step, traveler. It's dark, I know. It's been dark in Millbrook since before I was born.

I'm Sister Wren. I patch people up. You're from one of the new keeps, aren't you? You have that look. Like someone who has started counting to three.

buttons.name: I have an old journal. Do you know it?

scenes.text:
Let me see. Red leather, the royal seal... and the name cut off the cover. Put that away. Now, please.

The knights burned every book that king ever touched, and his son's after him. Whoever put that one in your pack wanted it to outlive them.

I won't ask where you got it. I notice you don't know either.

If I knew his name I wouldn't say it in a house with a well. Read old Quill's chronicle, if you can find a volume the Order missed. Chroniclers write down who was whose father. It's most of what they do.

And read the journal itself. A man tells you who he is by what frightens him.

Every third night they come for your walls. You've noticed. Everyone with walls notices.

Nobody here will tell you why, because nobody here knows. The knights know. Ask a knight and watch his face go smooth as a plate.

The clocks. Six of them, and every one reads the same minute. Old Reeve Tock stopped them, long ago, and the night stopped with them.

People here like it. In the dark you can't see who is facing the wall.

The Reeve left a statement in the clock tower. Read it before you go asking villagers which clock is which. Some of them will lie to you.

The first one? Now that IS the question, and I'll tell you what my mother told me. The Reeve started with the clock in the

Traveler?

Traveler, your nose is bleeding. Look at me. Look at ME, not at the wall, what are you looking at the w

There you are. THERE you are. Sit. Sit down.

You went grey as tallow, and then the chair was empty. I counted. Nine. Then you were in it again, wet to the skin, and my floor is bone dry.

I have seen that once before. I was nine years old and it was my brother. He was gone the whole night.

Don't tell me what you saw. I can see it on you. It wasn't anywhere, was it? Nowhere on any map of ours. I can smell the water on you.

I don't have a name for it. I think the knights do, and I think they've spent three hundred years making sure nobody else does.

All I know is that it let go of you. It didn't let go of Tobin. Stay away from the well tonight.

You are not fine. Your sleeves are dripping and you're holding that cup in your left hand. You came in here right-handed.

...There. It's passing. You've switched back. Saints, I hoped I'd never watch that happen twice.

It let go of you. It didn't let go of my brother. I'd like to know why, and so should you.

The first clock. I was about to say, wasn't I, before you... went.

I find I've lost the nerve to say it out loud. Maybe that was the point. Read the Reeve's statement in the tower, then ask the villagers which clock he stopped first. All six will answer. One of them will be lying, and you'll know which once you've heard the other five.

The Ashen Gate keep a chapterhouse east of the Vale road. Grey banners. They used to keep a waystation here too, by the mill. It's empty now, but they left in a hurry, and people who leave in a hurry leave things in cupboards.

Forget I said it.

...No. You have kind eyes, and I am tired of forgetting things on purpose. Come back when you've read something about the Lost Days. Then you'll know what to ask me, and I'll know you're serious.
Still dark, still here. What do you need?
You again. Good. Wipe your feet, somebody has to pretend it's morning.
Hold this. No, the other end. Now. What is it?
I've a pot on and a boy with a fever. Talk while I work.

You say those words like someone who has heard them, not someone who has read them.

There's a notice in the square about it. The Reeve's office wants everyone to know there is no cause for alarm. Read it. Then tell me if you believe it.

buttons.name: I read it. It's a lie.

scenes.text: Ask, then. Quietly.

buttons.name: How do I tell the Returned?

scenes.text:
My brother. He was eleven. He went to the well on a third night and came home in the morning, and my mother said he was only tired.

He lived in our house for forty more years. He was kind to me every day of them. He was not my brother.

I wrote it down when I was nine, so I would never talk myself out of it. It's in a box under my stairs.

Take it. I know it by heart. Put it somewhere it will be kept. That is all I ever wanted for it.

Three things. My mother's generation knew them and were fined two silver for saying so.

I won't hand them to you. You'll find them written in more than one place, by people who never met each other, and that is how you'll know they're true. Write in your Ledger when you're sure what the Returned are.

Down. Tobin went to the well. In Rimehold they walked out onto the lake. In Gull's Rest it was the sea.

Always water, always the third night. If you want to know more about the lake, there's a woman in Rimehold called Sigrun whose grandmother followed the footprints.

You worked it out. I can see it on you.

Then you know my real brother has been singing under that well for longer than I've been alive. If you ever get down there, traveler: his name is Tobin Ashby. Say it to them. I think they forget.

You saw one. No, don't, I can tell. I saw one too. From the chapterhouse roof, on the east road, standing in the wheat. It did not flatten the wheat.

I reported it. I wrote it out properly, time and place and what it looked like, the way they teach us. The Grandmaster's clerk read it in front of me and put it on the fire and asked if there was anything else.

I said no, sir. God help me, I said no, sir, and I saluted.

I have been thinking about that since. Not the thing in the wheat. The clerk. He wasn't surprised. He had the look of a man who has burned that page before.

We are sworn to stand between the people and the dark. I did not know there was a part of the dark we had agreed not to mention.

buttons.name: Ask Brother Cael about a drawer.

scenes.text:
Hold. Sir Aldous Vane, Order of the Ashen Gate.

A light fell near this keep last night. Pale, about so big, and it hums. I am charged to take it into the Order's keeping. Have you seen it?

buttons.name: Why does the Order want it?

scenes.text:
A fallen star. That is what I was told and that is what I will tell you.

...It did not look like a star to me either. Stars do not whisper. But a knight of the Gate does not ask what lies below. It is the second line of the Rule.

buttons.name: Why does the Order want it?

scenes.text:
"If ever a light falls from below, a knight shall ride to it and take it, before it takes anyone." That is the Rule.

From below. I have always thought that a strange word to use about something that fell out of the sky.

Every knight carries a copy. Take mine, I know it by heart. If you would rather swear to it than fight beside it, come to the chapterhouse, east of the Vale road.

And if you find that light: do not pick it up with your bare hand.
Well met again. The roads are worse every month. What can I do for you?
You look tired. So do I. Nobody warns you about the paperwork.
Ah, good, a face that isn't asking me for a horse. Go on.
I have the watch in an hour. Until then I am yours.

We were eleven hundred once. We are eleven now. We keep the Gate shut and the ash cold, and we watch the keeps.

If you want our history, ask Brother Cael in the archive. He will give you the version we give to guests. Ask him twice and he may give you another.

Bandits. Illagers out of the badlands, the restless dead, sellswords. It is a lawless age.

Every third night. Yes. I have noticed that too. I asked the Grandmaster once and he looked at me the way my father did when I asked where the dog had gone.

Our founder. A shepherd's daughter from the hills above Bellhollow, marked on the palm by the saints. There's a shrine there, and a little book of her life in every chapel of ours.

She never wept, they say. I have always found that the saddest thing about her.

Your hand. Show me your hand.

...Saints. You picked it up.

I am supposed to bring you in. I am supposed to bring you to the Inquisitors. I have known you since the morning after your first siege and I find I am not drawing my sword. Go. Before I remember my oath.

buttons.name: What will it do to me?

scenes.text:
I don't know. That is the truth and it shames me. We take the lights and we are never told what becomes of them.

There was a mage, once. The Order burned him. They say his students hid his notebooks all over Aldmere. If anyone wrote down what you are now, it was him.

You've read it. The Grandmaster's own hand. "Let them think it is bandits."

I have told forty keeps it was bandits. I told YOU it was bandits. I believed it.

Give me a little time. A man cannot put down his whole life in one afternoon.

There is a vault under the chapterhouse they call the Burned Archive. I have stood guard on its door a hundred nights and never once asked what was behind it.

Brother Cael has the key. Tell him I sent you. Tell him I'm asking now.

She was his daughter. Our saint overthrew her own father, put him down a hole alive, and built us to stand on the lid.

I thought I would be angry at her. I think she was seventeen, and watched her people get out of bed and walk into the water every third night, and did a terrible thing to stop it. Then she lied for the rest of her life so no one would undo it. I don't know if she was right. I don't think she knew.

I'm with you. Whatever is at the bottom of this, I'm with you.

Don't tell me. I can smell it on your coat. Cold stone and the inside of a bell.

So they've come up the long way and walked to your wall on their own feet. Well. I wondered if I'd live to see that again, and it turns out I live to see everything.

Sit. You'll want to know what it was, and I'm not going to tell you, and you'll want to know why not.

Because you'd go home thinking you understood it, and that's how people get careless at gates.

I'll give you what's safe. It wasn't angry at you. Did you notice? Your raiders hate you, it's all over them. That one didn't. It walked up to your wall the way a man walks up to a field he's been told to measure.

It was sent to look. Something wanted to know how high you build.

There. That's the right question, and you asked it in the right order, after the fright and before the bragging.

Keep asking it. Ask the bell-keepers and the grey brothers and that girl on the ice. They've each got a piece and they each think it's the whole.

I've got a piece too. You'll get it when it won't kill you.

Wipe your feet. Not there. THERE.

I'm Mag. I'm three hundred and eleven years old. Go on, laugh. They all do. Then they ask for something for a cough.

So is an army marching on your walls every third night with nobody leading it. Yet here you are, with mud from a keep on your boots.

Come back when you've seen something impossible and stopped arguing with it.

Marsh mallow root, honey, don't breathe the fog after dark. Two emeralds, which I'll waive, because you asked a sensible question in a house full of nonsense.

Now. Do you want the cough cure, or do you want to know why I'm old?

Stop. Stand there. Don't come in yet.

...Oh, child. You picked it up. I can hear it on you from across the room, like a wet finger on a glass.

Well. It's done, and nobody is going to teach you, because the last man who could is ash. But I was his prentice and I was a nosy one. Take this. I wrote it when I was eleven. I understood about a third of it then and I wish I'd kept it that way.

Everything he let slip about what your sort can do. Fourteen of them, he counted. It won't tell you how. He never told ME how. It'll tell you what happened to the people who found out.

Read the third one twice. Read the tenth one before you get proud of yourself.

And some of them you'll not manage until you've been somewhere or met someone. The book says where, if you squint.
You again. Seen anything impossible yet?

Hm. You said that like you meant it.

I was twelve when they burned my teacher. He was the King's mage. You won't find the King in any book the knights let you read, either. I ran into the fen with a satchel and a head full of things I didn't understand, and something under the swamp took a liking to me, and I stopped getting older.

Here. My testimony. Wrote it myself, for the day someone believed me.
Sit. Ask. Don't touch the jars.

buttons.name: The day they took the king.

scenes.text: You're letting the damp out. In or out.

buttons.name: The day they took the king.

scenes.text: Back, are you. The frogs said you would be.

buttons.name: The day they took the king.

scenes.text: I was asleep. I've been asleep since Tuesday. Which Tuesday, I couldn't say. Ask.

buttons.name: The day they took the king.

scenes.text:
What did you say?

Say it again. Slowly.

..."Like a trowel." He said that to me the morning I was nine, the first day, in front of all eleven of the others, and I cried, and he gave me his own pen and never asked for it back.

Three hundred years. I thought I was waiting to see what came back out of that Crack. I think I was only waiting to be told off one more time.

Sit down, child. I've a notebook under the bed I've been denying for a long while.

I was eleven, and small enough to be under the cart.

They'll tell you she threw him in. She didn't throw him. Nobody threw that man anywhere. They walked him down into the valley to the Crack with his hands tied, and at the edge he asked them to cut the rope, and the girl nodded, and they cut it.

He turned round once. He was looking for her face. She had already put her back to him.

Then he walked in. Upright. Like a man going down to his own cellar.

And then nothing. That's what I'm telling you, child. No scream. No fall. I've seen folk die every way there is to do it, and that wasn't one of them.

Three hundred years I've kept myself going on roots and spite. Did you never wonder what I was waiting to see come back out?

Corvin Hale. Rude, brilliant, never washed. He wrote ten notebooks and twelve of us carried them off in twelve directions the night before the fire. A hunter with hounds got eleven of us.

The notebooks are still out there. His tower in the Vale hills, the north lake, the lighthouse, the desert vault. One of them is under my bed and I will deny it.

I never said that.

...Fine. Notebook Three. It's the one about the moon. It's the only one I ever understood. Take it. Bring the rest together some day, all ten on one shelf, and come and tell me. I have waited three hundred years to hear someone say they did.

"What the carving shows, the sky must not." He made us chant it.

There's a door in the north, at the Rimehold lake. A shrine with a moon cut into it. One of us went through that door with the hunter behind her. I don't know which of them I feel sorrier for.

Five of them have lost days. Four of those came back as themselves, only frightened. One didn't.

I know which. I won't say. If I name it, it runs, and the Mother makes another. You'll have to catch it in a lie. Talk to all five. A shape wears the person like a borrowed glove. It gets the small things wrong.

Choir scripture. It's written right to left, the way they wrote before there was an Aldmere. Don't read it at night and don't read it aloud.

There's one carved inside the well bucket here. I copied it out fair, years ago. You may have it if you promise not to hum.

All ten. On one shelf. You did it.

...Give me a moment.

He told me one thing he never wrote down, because he was afraid of who might read it. This land had another name, before the bells. He never learned it. But he knew who still uses it: they do. It's in one of their hymns, and their hymns sometimes wash up.

This washed up in my fen forty years ago. I've never dared read it. You do it.

Mind the lamp. Don't stand between it and the sea.

I'm the keeper. Elias. Forgive me, I'm writing to my wife, and I lose the thread if I stop.

Out. She went down to the strand to see the seabed, the night the sea drew back. She'll be home when she can see the light.

The parish register says a fever. The parish register is wrong. I've told them and told them.

Oh... a little while ago. The night the war ended.

Which war? THE war. The Grey Host. Their ships were lying on the sand like dead whales.

You're looking at me the way the new priest does.

Letters. I put them in bottles, mostly. The sea brings some back and the gulls take others. You'll find them up and down this coast if you look.

You won't be able to read them. Annet and I wrote in a cipher of our own when we were courting, so her father couldn't. There was a brass wheel for it. I lost mine years ago, somewhere inland.

Two rings of letters, one turning inside the other. A scholar's toy. I lent it to a man from the Vale who was collecting old books, and he never brought it back.

If you keep books yourself, look between them. That's where such things end up.
Mind the lamp. Oh, it's you. Did you find any of my letters?
Mind the lamp. Have you read them? Any of them? I'd like to know someone has.
Is that the tide or is that you? Come up, come up.
Careful on the stair. It has one more step than it used to.
I was just writing to her. It will keep. What can I tell you?

Once a month, when the moon is dark, the sea goes out nearly as far as it did that night. You can see the tower of Saint Brannoc's from here.

I have the place worked out to the very stone. It's all in the seventh letter. I keep meaning to go.

I never told anyone that. You must have read the fifth.

He was very polite. He was soaked and he wasn't cold. He held his sword in his left hand, and I remember thinking: that's not right, the coins all show him right-handed.

I've never said whose face it was. I'm not going to now.

Because she has to find the shore.

People say things come up the beach on the third night. That they follow the light. Annet herself said it, in a dream I had.

It was only a dream. I can't put it out. If I put it out she'll never find me.

You've seen her. Don't tell me how she looked.

...She said to put it out. She said she wasn't angry.

She always sang a little sharp, you know. I could pick her out of a hundred voices.

There's one more letter. I left it where I said I'd go. Read it, and then come back, and I'll do what she asked.

So now you know what I am. A habit that kept climbing the stairs after the man went down them.

She's free? Then it's time.

Would you do it? I don't think my hands can. Just close the shutter. Thank you. It was a long watch. It was a very long watch.

Oh, thank goodness, you're in one piece. I watched from the upstairs window. Well. I watched from under the upstairs window, with a book over my head, but I heard a great deal.

Now, I have been through the shelves since four this morning and I want to show you something that is not there. Sieges, raiders, the Grey Host, every third night, there are pages and pages. A tall thing with no face that the raiders bow to? Not a line. Not one.

That's what I thought! For about an hour. Then I started looking at what's been cut.

There are pages gone from four of our books, all near the end, all in chapters about the last year of a siege somewhere. Cut with a blade, neatly, by somebody who cared about the binding.

So people have seen them. And then somebody tidied up. A missing page is still a clue, you know. It tells you which way the scissors were facing.

A librarian, I'm sorry to say. Somebody trained. Somebody with a house style.

I used to work for people with a house style.

If you find a book out in the world with its last pages still in it, bring it to me before you bring it to anyone in grey. I'll make you a copy and hide the copy.

Sit down, sit down. I've been cataloguing what people TOLD you instead of what you shelved, and I don't like where the cards have ended up.

Card one. A king was overthrown, and the Order that burned forty-one of his portraits never paid for a grave.

Card two. He went into the Crack alive, on his own two feet.

Card three. Those below have no names, and yet they have given one to somebody. Morvane.

I'm an archivist. I don't draw conclusions, I file them. But I've only the one drawer left, and all three cards fit in it.

No. You say it. Your Ledger has a page for it, "Who Is Morvane?", and it wants a name in your own hand.

And if we're right, then when you stand in front of him at last, look at his eyes, and at which hand he uses. The old journal in your pack describes a right-handed boy. Master Quill says the King came back from below using his left. I should like to know which of them is still in there.

Oh! A keep with shelves. Do you know how rare that is? The Order threw me out for reading, and I've been walking ever since looking for somewhere that keeps books instead of burning them.

Pell. Archivist, formerly Novice. I'll catalogue for my supper.

Build Archive Shelves at your Siege Workshop. Hold a Lore Tome and click a shelf to shelve it. Click a shelf with an empty hand to open the catalogue: read anything you've shelved, take tomes back out, and claim what you've earned.

Finish a whole collection and something always turns up. The Library grows, too: at ten tomes, at twenty-five. Old books keep secrets in their bindings.

Everywhere somebody once had a reason to hide one. Chapels. Ruins. Under floors. The great beasts of each region carry one, and things that walk at night sometimes drop them.

A tome you've found leaves the next reader's copy where it was, so nobody can strip the land bare. But a tome on your shelf is yours, and a thief with a Breaching Charge might disagree.
Catalogue's up to date. What are we puzzling over?

buttons.name: How do I solve a thread?

scenes.text: Don't move that pile, it's in an order. What have you found?

buttons.name: How do I solve a thread?

scenes.text: Oh, it's you! I was hoping it was you and not a draught.

buttons.name: How do I solve a thread?

scenes.text: Ink's wet, mind your sleeve. Go on, what's the question?

buttons.name: How do I solve a thread?

scenes.text:
Good! They're supposed to. Ask three things of any book. Who wrote it? Who were they afraid of? And were they there?

Master Quill wrote what the court told him, but he couldn't stop himself noting the small true things. The Order wrote what it wanted believed. The mage wrote what he saw and was burned for it. Weigh them accordingly.

Two kinds of unreadable. If it's scrambled letters, it's a cipher, and you need a Cipher Wheel in your pack. If the letters are fine but the words run backward, it's Hollow writing, right to left, and you need a Tide Glass. Or, ahem, a certain kind of hand.

Both turn up in a well-stocked Library sooner or later.

The catalogue lists every tome you're missing with a note on where such a thing would be kept. Open it at any shelf and look for the grey entries.

If you want my advice: finish the Testimonies first. Ordinary people notice more than chroniclers.

Brother Fennick's field notes! Six notebooks, each stating one true thing about the place where the Gate now sits: water, bells, hands, cold, salt, roots.

Visit the seven places with the notes in hand and strike off the ones that don't fit. When all six are on your shelf you may Name the Thin Place in the catalogue. Name it wrong and you'll lose days. Name it right and you'll have found a thing the Order lost.

Your Ledger of Whispers copies down every clue you read, sorted by the mystery it belongs to. When a thread has enough clues, it asks you a question.

Some questions give you choices. The best ones make you write the answer yourself. A wrong answer closes the thread for a day, so read before you guess.

Seventy-four. Every one. I counted three times and then I sat down on the floor.

They burned all of this, you know. Forty-one portraits and every chronicle they could find, and you put it back, book by book, on your own shelves.

You don't need an archivist any more. I'll stay anyway, if that's all right. I like it here.

buttons.name: Stay as long as you like.

scenes.text:
Close the door, please. All the way.

You are going to describe something to me and I am going to tell you the Order has no record of it. Both of us will know what that is worth. So let me save you the breath. Taller than a man. Nothing where the face goes. The raiders made way.

There is a drawer in this room with no label on it. I was told to burn what is in it forty years ago. I am a slow worker.

Eleven reports. The oldest is three hundred years old and the newest is a good deal younger than I am. A reeve, two priests, a child, a knight of this house. None of them knew about the others. They all draw the same thing in the margin, badly.

And every one of them was written in the season before a village stopped answering letters.

I am not telling you this to frighten you. I am telling you because you are the twelfth, and you are the first one who came and asked.

buttons.name: What does the Order call them?

scenes.text:
Officially, nothing. A thing with no name cannot be in a report, and a thing in no report did not happen. That is very nearly our whole method.

Unofficially the old brothers called them the tall company. As in, "he keeps tall company these nights." They said it about men who had stopped sleeping.

Go home and sleep. I mean it kindly.

The reading room is open to guests. The archive is not. Please don't lean on the shelves.

You may read the Chronicle volume on the lectern. We keep that one on display. You'll see why.

Because it says what we need it to say. "The Treachery of the Mage." Master Quill wrote twelve volumes. We display one.

Read the last line of it carefully. "I have been told to set it down plainly, and I have." A chronicler doesn't write that sentence by accident.

Burned. Officially.

Unofficially, a book is a hard thing to burn completely when the man holding the torch can read. My predecessors had a way of finding that a volume had been 'lost' in a village chapel or a ruined nursery.

I didn't say that. Good day.

Our history. "On the Kingless Years." It will tell you there was never a king called Oswin and that the name is a peasant's mistake for a saint's day.

I copy it out fresh every ten years, so that it will last. I have very neat handwriting. It is the only part of the task I can be proud of.
The reading room is open. The archive is not. I say this every day. Some days I even mean it.
Quietly, please. The books are used to it.
You came back. Most people need only one look at this room.
I have misfiled something on purpose today. It was very satisfying. Yes?

There is a list. There is always a list: an Order that burns things without an inventory is just a mob.

It's kept below, in the place it describes. I am not permitted to take guests there. I would need a knight of the Gate to ask me.

Tried for calling the Grey Host down on Aldmere with his bells. He arrived at court two years AFTER the Host landed. The tribunal did not find that worth noting.

His cell is still here, downstairs. Nobody has ever cleaned it. I think nobody could bear to.

One man's. Forty-one portraits, a great seal, a coronation robe, a child's wooden horse with a name cut in the belly. All burned, all listed.

I will tell you what is not on the list, because I have read it more often than my prayers. A coffin. A shroud. A gravedigger's fee. The Order kept receipts for the lamp oil it used that week. It did not pay to bury a king.

I do not know what that means. I know what I think on the third nights.

That a man nobody buried is a man nobody saw die.

I didn't say that either. Good day.

You've come from below. No, don't tell me, it's in how you're standing. Sit. Let an old man say something aloud in this building once before he dies.

Morvane was King Oswin. Aldric's son. The boy in that journal of yours, nine years old and afraid of nothing. He made a peace with the Hollow and he kept it, and for that his own daughter put him through the Crack alive, took a saint's name, and founded this Order to burn his face off the world so that nobody would know him if he ever came back up.

He did not come back up. They crowned him down there instead. Every third night for three hundred years, that was him. Knocking.

Then it was his to give, and he gave it to you. I wonder what he hoped you would do with it.

Master Quill wrote twelve volumes and we display one. I am going to write the thirteenth. Plainly, this time, and nobody will have to tell me to.

Thank you. Lean on the shelves if you like.

Aldous sent you. Aldous is asking.

Forty years I've waited for one of them to ask. I thought it would be someone cleverer, to be truthful. I'm glad it was someone kind.

The stair is behind the third shelf. Take the inventory. It's time somebody other than me had read it.

You've seen the list. Forty-one portraits. I used to recite it at night, like a rosary.

Two things on it were never found: the mage's notebooks and the chronicler's last volume. And one thing was never ON it, because nobody knew to look. Our saint wrote a letter she never sent. If it exists, it's wherever she went to grieve. Where does a daughter go to grieve?

You've the look. Sit down before you fall down.

Tall. No face. Walked like it was remembering how. And your raiders stood aside for it.

Gran had a word for those and I'll not teach it you, it does no good in a mouth. But I'll tell you what she said. She said the Host never crossed the water with anything like that. They met it here. On the last night. It was the last thing any of them looked at.

Something did. At seventeen past three, six thousand men, and not a boot left on the grass.

So think on this, southerner. Whatever is sending raiders at your wall every third night has been sending men. Other people's men. Angry and borrowed. Last night it sent one of its own.

You don't do that until you've stopped being careful.

buttons.name: Why would it stop being careful?

scenes.text:
Because it's nearer than it was. That's all I've got. I'm a fisherman's daughter with a bad shoulder.

Count your ravens tonight. If there's more of them than yesterday, they know something too.

Shut the door, you're letting the cold in.

You'll be wanting the lake. Southerners always want the lake. Go and look, then. Don't walk to the middle.

Cousin Wren. Still patching people up in the dark? Good. We Ashbys are spread thin since the Lost Days, but we keep count of each other.

Sit. If Wren sent you, you get the long version.

Three hundred years back, half of Rimehold got out of bed on one night and walked onto the ice. My grandmother's grandmother's... it goes on a while... followed the prints at dawn. They go to the middle and stop.

Gran wrote down what her gran told her. It's up in my rafters. Take it down yourself, I've a bad shoulder.

Because that's where they stopped.

And because some nights, if you stand there and look straight down, there are lights under the ice. Towers. A town. Not ours. Nobody ever built a town down there.
Door. Shut. What is it?

buttons.name: Why did the Grey Host come?

scenes.text: You'll want feeding. Southerners always do. Talk first.

buttons.name: Why did the Grey Host come?

scenes.text: Boots off or stay by the door. What now?

buttons.name: Why did the Grey Host come?

scenes.text: Lake's still there, if that's what you came to check.

buttons.name: Why did the Grey Host come?

scenes.text:
You've been reading. Nobody asks that who hasn't.

We don't tell southerners this. My people were the Host. The ones who stayed behind with the wounded, anyway. And the old women say nobody ordered that crossing. There was a sound under the ice, one winter, like a bell a long way down, and every fighting man on the Isles got up and started sharpening things. Couldn't have told you why. Couldn't have stopped.

Gran said you never hear it with your ears. You hear it with whatever part of you is already angry.

Every third night. You've got walls, you know that better than I do.

There's a name goes with it now, in the newer verses. I'll not say it indoors.

If you ever find you can make that sound yourself, and I've a feeling about you, think hard about who you'd be copying.

Ours. Every man of the Isles fed one from his own hand, and it was said that if you died abroad your raven carried your name home.

When the Host cut down one of your bells they nailed a raven up in its place, and you southerners took it for spite. It was a trade. A voice for a voice. They'd been told to take the bells, and some part of them was still decent enough to leave something.

Now there's six thousand birds that flew home that winter with no names to carry. They've not known what to do with themselves since.

So they do the one thing they've left. They go where the Host is going next, and they get there first, and they wait.

If you see ravens on your wall at dusk, count them. Then bar the gate.

...Fine. Stand in the doorway. Half out.

Morvane. There. The verses say he sits at the middle of it, and the rest go quiet when he speaks.

But here's what Gran had from her gran. Those below don't have names. Not one of them, not ever. They've no use for them. So if there's a name down there, they made it for somebody who came to them needing one. Somebody who'd lost his own.

Now shut the door. You're letting it listen.

Somebody who had it burned off every wall in the country, I'd think.

Ask the knights whose that was. They kept a list. They always keep a list.

Older than the village. There's a moon cut into it, round and full. Folk go out on the full moon and leave offerings and nothing happens, and they go home pleased that nothing happened.

Gran used to say, "it's the other one you want." She said it the way you'd say it about a spoon.

The knights kept a hunting lodge on the far shore. A man with white hair and a pack of hounds, hunting people, the story goes. He went out on the ice one night and the hounds came back without him.

Nobody goes in. Nobody's stopping you.

I've seen it. Once. I was nine.

There was no moon at all that night, black as a boot. But I looked down, and there was a moon IN the ice, full and white, right under the shrine. And the ice by it had a seam in it, like a door ajar.

I ran home. I'd run home again.

So you've worked out the moon. Then you're going down there.

If you see people facing the walls of houses that look like ours: the Ashbys who walked were Hild's brother Orm, and his three girls. I'd take it kindly if you told them the family still keeps count.

Welcome to Sunscar. Water is two emeralds a skin, shade is free, and before you ask: the wind.

The statues. Everyone asks. The desert wind wore the faces away. It's in the town record.

buttons.name: All of them? Only the faces?

scenes.text:
Kings. Old ones. Nobody remembers which.

There are forty statues on the avenue and one face between them. I mean, there WAS one face. They were all the same man. At different ages. I shouldn't know that. You can tell from the hands.

...The wind doesn't take a nose and leave the fingers. I know. I've been warden for twenty years. I've had a long time to look at them.

The record says what it says. You're welcome to read it. It also says not to look for the fragments, because there aren't any.
Water, shade, or statues?
Sunscar thanks you for your visit. I am required to say so. What do you want?
Mind the statues on your way out. They were here first.
I have a petition about a goat and then I have you. Go on.
You again. You've got me looking at them on my rounds now. I hope you're pleased.

My father was warden before me. He used to say a careful man scatters things where he can find them again.

A brow under the old cistern. A jaw in the east tower. An eye where the caravans water. I don't know the rest, and I don't know that, either, officially.

The Seneschal. Lord Sorrel. He's been Seneschal as long as there's been a Sunscar, they say, which is just the kind of thing people say.

Nobody sees him. He keeps to the lower fortress. He wears a helm. Always has. My father never saw his face either.

There's a heraldry riddle on the vault door under the fortress. "Grey eyes over a laughing mouth, the right hand raised." Children here skip rope to it.

I always took it for a rhyme. It's a description, isn't it. It's instructions.

He did it himself. With a mason's chisel. So the last hands on that face would be gentle ones.

Twenty years I've told travelers it was the wind.

I'm changing the town record. Let the Order come and argue with me. Thank you for making me look.

Two loaves is all that's left. He's baking less.

You're the one from the keep. Sister Wren says you look at things properly. Would you look at something for me? It's my husband. Don't turn round. He's in the back.

Harl went out for flour four nights back and came home at dawn, damp, saying the road was long. It's a mile.

He's kind as ever. Kinder. He remembered my name-day, which he never has in nineteen years.

But he took the bell off the shop door. Said it gave him a head. And I came down in the night and he was stood in the pantry. Just stood. With his face to the wall.

Wren told me the three things, and I wish she hadn't.

The hand. Harl's right-handed, always was.

The wall. When they think nobody's by, they turn and face it.

And bells. They can't bear one. Ring one close and they... go home, she said. She wouldn't say where home was.

Watch him knead. Watch him when the shop's empty. Then come and tell me, and tell me true.
Well? Have you watched him?

buttons.name: Tell me again what to look for.
He's your husband. He's only tired.

scenes.text: Loaves are a penny. You're not here for loaves, are you.

buttons.name: Tell me again what to look for.
He's your husband. He's only tired.

scenes.text: Keep your voice down, he's only through there.

buttons.name: Tell me again what to look for.
He's your husband. He's only tired.

scenes.text: I've been counting how long he stands at the back door. Ask me how long.

buttons.name: Tell me again what to look for.
He's your husband. He's only tired.

scenes.text:
...No. No, it isn't, is it.

He kneads with his left. I've known since the second morning. I wanted someone else to say it so it wouldn't be me.

The awful thing is he doesn't know. He thinks he's Harl. He asked me this morning why I was crying and he meant it.

There's a hand-bell on the chapel step. I can't. Would you? Or don't. I don't know which I'm asking.

Tired. Yes. That'll be it. The road, and the damp.

Thank you. You've no idea. I'll make him a posset and we'll say no more about it.

I still set two places. He still sits at one, some nights. I've stopped coming down to look.

You told me true. I asked you to. Take a loaf.

You said he was tired.

The bed was empty this morning and there were wet footprints to the well, and none back. And the pantry wall's damp at the height of a man's face.

I don't blame you. I wanted to hear it. Next time somebody asks you, look harder.

You. Southerner. You've been asking about the lake, so you know what comes out of it.

My father went through the ice at midwinter. We had him out inside a hundred breaths. He's not been the same and I need someone who isn't kin to tell me what he is.

He mends with his left hand now. Seventy years a right-handed man.

He sits with his face to the shed wall, hours at a time.

You know what that makes him, round here. There's men saying we should take him out on the ice with the fishing bell and be done. I've an axe by the door that says they won't. But I have to know.

buttons.name: I'll go and look at him.
What does the dog make of him?

scenes.text:
The dog? Sleeps on his feet. Same as ever.

...Why? What's the dog to do with it?

buttons.name: I'll go and look at him.

scenes.text: Well? You've seen him. What is he?

buttons.name: What does the dog make of him?
He's your father. Leave him be.

scenes.text: Mind the nets. Well? I've not slept.

buttons.name: What does the dog make of him?
He's your father. Leave him be.

scenes.text: He asked after you this morning. By name. I don't know what to make of that.

buttons.name: What does the dog make of him?
He's your father. Leave him be.

scenes.text: Tell me you've watched him. Tell me something.

buttons.name: What does the dog make of him?
He's your father. Leave him be.

scenes.text:
Say why. I'll need to say it to the others.

...His right arm hangs. Aye. Since the ice. I'd taken it for stubbornness. And the wall's where the lamp hook is, and his eyes are going. And he rings the dawn bell himself, every morning, same as he has since before I was born. Would one of them do that?

Gods. I nearly let them take a sick old man out on the lake.

You've done my house a good turn. Left hand and a wall, and I was ready to believe it. That's how it gets you, isn't it. It doesn't even have to send one.

Then that's that.

...I'll do it myself. He taught me the knots. It should be me.

He's in the shed. Swearing at a net with his wrong hand. Dog on his feet.

Go in and say good day. He likes you. He says you look at things properly.

We rang the fishing bell at him on the ice. He put his good hand over his ear and asked me what in the cold hells I was doing.

He's forgiven me. I've not. Get out of my shed.

That's my brother. Pip. He's six.

You're going to look at him and then you're going to look at me. Grown-ups do. So I'll save you the bother. Yes. I know.

He went off the rocks in the spring. Third night. I was meant to be minding him.

He walked back up the beach in the morning. Wet. Smiling. Mam screamed the whole street awake, she was that glad.

He throws with his left now. He doesn't like the chapel. When he thinks I'm asleep he gets up and stands by the wall on the sea side.

He's not Pip. He's ever so nice, though. He lets me win.

Mam sings again. She does his hair every morning. She didn't get out of bed for a month before he came back.

She doesn't know. Or she does and she's better at it than me.

Because you'd have worked it out. You've got a bell on your pack, or you'll get one. Everybody who works it out gets a bell.

I'm asking you not to. That's all. He's not hurting anybody. And the real Pip's not coming back whether you ring it or not, is he.

Is he?

buttons.name: Your mother has to be told.

scenes.text: Have you thought?

buttons.name: Your mother has to be told.

scenes.text: I saved you a place on the wall. It's the dry bit.

buttons.name: Your mother has to be told.

scenes.text: He's down there again. Look. Right on the line.

buttons.name: Your mother has to be told.

scenes.text: Did you decide? You don't have to say. I can tell if you've decided.

buttons.name: Your mother has to be told.

scenes.text:
...Thank you.

I do know it's not him. I say goodnight to the real one after. Out the window. In case it carries.

Then you tell her. I'm not going to. And you ring it, if it's got to be rung. Not me.

I was minding him the first time. I'm not doing it twice.

He found a crab today. He named it after me.

You kept your word. Grown-ups mostly don't.

Mam knows now. She hasn't rung anything. She just does his hair slower.

I suppose you thought it was right. I suppose it might be.

Oh, thank goodness, someone with sense. Come in. No, stay there, the dog's in a mood, he's been in a mood for weeks.

It's my Odo. I think he's one of them. One of the ones that come back. Will you look at him for me? I daren't ask anyone in the village.

He looks at me strangely. Sideways. Like he's counting something.

He's taken to sleeping in the reed shed. He's taken the dog with him, and that dog was MINE, he was mine from a pup, and now he growls when I come near.

And Odo's started ringing the chapel bell of an evening. Every evening. He knows I can't abide it lately, it goes right through my head, and he rings it anyway and watches the house.

Something's wrong with him. You'll see it.

Old Mag says three things. The wrong hand. Standing to the wall. And they can't bear a bell.

Well, Odo's right-handed same as ever, I'll grant. And I've not caught him at a wall. But he's sly. He'd hide it.

Go round the back and watch him. I'll wait here. I like it here by the door-post, it's restful.
Did you see him? Did you see how he looks at the house?

buttons.name: Hesper. Which hand is your cup in?

scenes.text: You're back. Good. I've kept the tea warm, I don't know why.

buttons.name: Hesper. Which hand is your cup in?

scenes.text: He's out with the reeds. He's always out with the reeds now.

buttons.name: Hesper. Which hand is your cup in?

scenes.text: Tell me what you saw. Take your time. I've nothing but time.

buttons.name: Hesper. Which hand is your cup in?

scenes.text:
Himself? Then why does he look at me like that? Why did he take my dog?

...You're kind to say it. I expect you're right. I expect I'm tired. I haven't felt myself since the night I went out for the washing and the fog came down.

It was only a moment. I was only gone a moment.

I KNEW it. I knew. Oh, my poor Odo.

I'll tell the neighbours. They'll know what to do. They've a bell.

Thank you. Thank you. Mind the dog as you go, he's not been right.

My...

The left. It's in my left.

I'm right-handed. I've always been...

The dog. The bell. He isn't ringing it AT me. He's ringing it to see if I'll... And I've been stood at this door-post since noon, haven't I. Facing it.

Oh.

Oh, poor Odo. He's known for weeks. He's been sleeping in the shed and he still brings me my tea.

Don't tell him I know. Please. Let me have the winter. I'll go quiet in the spring, I promise. I'd just like to see him cut the reeds once more.

He brought me tea again this morning. I held it in my right. It took all my mind to do it, but I did, and he smiled.

Thank you for asking about the cup. Nobody else looked at ME.

Oh, it's you. I'm sorry, I can't talk, I've such a head. That bell.

It's restful here by the post. I'll just stand a while.

§7The pool is singing. Thousands of voices on one note.

One of them, somewhere near the bottom, is very slightly off it, and seems to be swearing.

You cannot make out the words. Someone with the art might.

No. No, no. Stand still. You're dripping warmth into it.

So it's you. The flat one. I've been listening to you murder those arts from down here for longer than I care to say, and now you've walked in, on legs, and you want to chat.

Well? Three hundred years I've held this note with every soul they ever took. Make it worth my dropping it.

I was burned. Thoroughly, at dawn, with my books. And then some careful soul put what was left into a river, on the theory that nothing could gather it.

Not one man on that tribunal had ever asked himself where rivers go.

Hale. Corvin Hale. I tuned the hundred bells of Crownhold and I held a lamp at a table of wet stone, and I was right about everything, and it did me no good at all.

buttons.name: Old Mag sent me, in a way.

scenes.text:
I wrote it down myself. "Those who walk down to them are not eaten. They are kept." I simply never expected to be evidence.

I'm not alive. I'm not gone. I am a note with opinions. It turns out that's most of what I was before.
Ask. Quickly. Every word I say to you is a word I'm not singing, and they notice.

buttons.name: What did the truce really say?
Who sits in the chair down here?

scenes.text: Stand still. The water carries better when you stand still.

buttons.name: What did the truce really say?
Who sits in the chair down here?

scenes.text: You again. Good. I had half a sentence saved for you and I've lost it. Ask.

buttons.name: What did the truce really say?
Who sits in the chair down here?

scenes.text: Speak low. I am borrowing this breath from a tune and it will be wanted back.

buttons.name: What did the truce really say?
Who sits in the chair down here?

scenes.text:
Three lines. I can still see his breath in the lamp.

They take back the army they called. Every third night is theirs: no bell is rung, they walk above as guests, and any of ours who wish may walk below. And it is sworn on their crown, not his, which he may not wear and they would not touch.

That's all. No souls. No firstborn. No trick. Everything that went wrong after went wrong on our side of the paper.

He was the only man at court who never laughed at me. Do you know how rare that is, for a king? They're raised to it.

He took their pledge in his bare right hand because it was offered to him, and it would have been rude to ask for a cloth. It bit him to the bone. He never used that hand again and he never once mentioned it.

At my trial I had one defence. "I remember him." It was true and it was sufficient and they burned me for it.

"Someone must." Yes. I ran out of candle. They came for me before I could find another.

You'll have imagined something grand. Someone must wear the crown. Someone must slay the thing.

It was: someone must go down and say good morning. That's the whole discovery. Thirty years, a hundred bells, and that's all of it. They had been knocking for four hundred years and nobody had answered the door.

A thing sworn can be sworn again. But only by someone who's first bothered to say hello.

...

Well.

That's the first time anyone's said it to me, as it happens. In either world.

Get out before I become sentimental. It puts me off the note.

Magda? The small one? She's ALIVE?

She was twelve. She carried the ninth notebook into a swamp in the dark with hounds behind her, and I never knew if...

Tell her this, exactly. Tell her she still holds a pen like a trowel. She'll know it's me. Nobody else was ever that rude to her.

No.

Not from me. I'll teach you every art there is and I'll tell you what was said at that table to the word. But who sits there is a thing you'll want to have worked out yourself, standing up, before you see him. It will matter to you that you did. It will matter to him.

You have all the pieces. Three people up there are each holding one. Go and be a nuisance to an archivist.

He's stopped.

I felt it go out of the note like a string cut. The whole Choir went a hair sharp. They don't know what to do without him. Neither do I, as it happens.

I held the lamp for him once, at the table. I should have liked to hold it at the end. I gather you did that instead, in your fashion. Was he...

No. Don't tell me. I remember him. That was always the point of me.

Of course he did. The red one. He used to read it on the walls on the third nights, when he thought no one could see.

The chair's empty now, and it wants someone who can hear all of this at once and not break. If that's to be you, then listen to an old flat voice: keep the truce. It was a good one. It was only ever kept by one man.
